results.statement: Explain what an AI management system is and what a management system standard does

primary.reason: States the standard specifies requirements for an AI management system within an organization's context and applies to any organization providing or using AI products/services.
Gives the defining formula of a management system: interrelated elements establishing policies, objectives and processes.
Core requirement to establish, implement, maintain, continually improve and document the AIMS including its processes and interactions.
States continual improvement of the AIMS's suitability, adequacy and effectiveness, anchoring the PDCA concept.
States Annex A controls are a reference, not all mandatory, supporting the distinction between management system requirements and controls.
States the AIMS is applicable to any organization and gives an AI-technology-specific view versus technology-neutral management system standards.
States 42006 adds requirements to 17021-1 for bodies auditing and certifying an AIMS — the certification basis.
Explicit definition of AIMS as interrelated elements establishing policies, objectives and processes for provision, development or use of AI systems.
States it contains requirements for bodies certifying management systems, explaining why organization-level certification is possible.

dropped.why: Bare terminology entry for 'policy'; states nothing about the AIMS or what a management system standard does.
Generic definition of 'objective' with discipline examples; not a statement about the management system concept.
Generic definition of 'process' only; nothing testable for this task.
Turns out to be the scope-determination requirement (boundaries, documented scope), belonging to the context task.
Guidance on integrating the AIMS with ISO/IEC 27001, 27701, 9001, not on what an AIMS or MSS is.
Definition of certification audit with joint/combined/integrated audit notes — audit-type material, not the AIMS concept.

results.note: PDCA is described in the 42001 Introduction, which is not a numbered clause in the list; clause 4.4 and 10.1 are the closest normative anchors.

results.statement: Determine the organization's roles with respect to its AI systems

primary.reason: States the shall-requirement to determine roles and enumerates provider, producer, customer, partner, subject and authority categories.
Explicitly requires documenting parties and their roles and ties role to PII controller/processor obligations, the data-processing element of the task knowledge.

dropped.why: Text is about boundaries/applicability of the AIMS scope and documented scope; never mentions roles.
Generic preamble that Annex A controls are a reference and need not all be used; says nothing about roles.
Generic statement that Annex B is non-mandatory implementation guidance; no role content.
Control statements on responsible use processes, objectives and intended use; does not state role-dependent applicability.
Control on apportioning responsibilities among third parties, not on determining the organization's own roles.
About certification scope being reflected in the SoA, not about AI role determination.
Audit time determination based on persons in the AI life cycle; unrelated to role categories.

results.note: 42001 Clause 3 does not define the role terms (they come from ISO/IEC 22989), so 4.1 is the anchor.

results.statement: Describe the AI system life cycle and why it anchors AIMS obligations

primary.reason: States the requirements/specification stage obligation, usable to key an activity-to-stage placement item.
States the design and development stage documentation obligation — a distinct life-cycle stage.
States the verification and validation stage obligation, distinguishable from deployment and operation.
States pre-deployment plan/requirements, anchoring the deployment stage.
States ongoing operation and monitoring obligations (monitoring, updates, support) — the post-release stage that defeats deploy-and-forget.
Requires determining which life-cycle phases need event logging, with a minimum of when the system is in use.
Objective explicitly states criteria and requirements are defined for each stage of the AI system life cycle.
Spells out deployment-stage content (release criteria, environment differences, sign-offs) for stage placement.
Explicitly addresses monitoring against production data and continuous-learning systems evolving in use.
Describes verification/validation activities (test data, release criteria) used to separate that stage from deployment.
States that life-cycle stages are considered and that the organization can specify its own stages against a generic model.
States risk sources arise across the entire life cycle from design to decommissioning — the core anchoring claim.
Requires implementation and monitoring of development-and-usage life cycle related controls, including control of changes.

dropped.why: About supplying technical documentation to categories of interested parties, not about life-cycle stages.
About setting responsible-development objectives; only mentions the development life cycle in passing.
Bare control requiring documented design/development processes; the life-cycle content lives in B.6.1.3.
Turned out to be about data quality and poisoning as ML risk sources, not life-cycle stages or drift.
One-line definition of maintainability; states nothing testable about stages, drift or retraining.
Concerns planned changes to the management system, not the AI system life cycle.
Generic AIMS monitoring and measurement clause; no life-cycle or drift content.
Uses 'AI life cycle' only to count personnel for audit-time determination.

results.note: ISO/IEC 5338 is a normative/bibliographic reference only; no clause in scope defines its stages, so life-cycle stage placement rests on A.6.2.x / B.6.2.x.
